title: Questions to Ask Before Your Root Canal Appointment
metaTitle: Questions to Ask Before a Root Canal Appointment
metaDescription: A practical checklist of questions to ask before a root canal — about diagnosis, alternatives, visits, crowns, aftercare, and cost — so you decide with confidence.

secondaryKeywords: what to ask dentist about root canal
excerpt: A patient's checklist of questions to ask before agreeing to a root canal, covering diagnosis, alternatives, the procedure, and aftercare.
heroImageAlt: A patient holding a checklist while talking with a dentist in a consultation room.
bodyHtml:
Before you agree to a root canal, the most useful questions to ask your dentist are about the diagnosis, your alternatives, what the treatment involves, how the tooth will be restored, and what to expect afterward. Asking these out loud helps you give informed consent and leaves you feeling confident rather than rushed. Below is a practical checklist you can bring to your appointment.

Why asking questions helps

A root canal is a common procedure, but it is still a decision about your own body, and you are entitled to understand it before going ahead. Patients who ask questions tend to feel calmer and more in control, partly because uncertainty is one of the biggest drivers of dental anxiety. A good dental team expects questions and answers them in plain language rather than rushing you toward a yes. There are no silly questions here, and if an explanation is unclear, it is always worth asking again until it genuinely makes sense to you. Writing your questions down beforehand can help, because it is easy to forget them once you are in the chair.

It also helps to bring someone with you if you feel nervous, and to let the team know if you would like extra time to think before deciding. Being an active participant in the conversation is not being difficult; it is exactly how informed consent is meant to work. The checklist below is grouped by theme so you can focus on the parts that matter most to you, whether that is understanding the diagnosis, weighing alternatives, or planning the practical details of your visits.

Questions about the diagnosis

  • Why do you think this tooth needs a root canal?
  • What did the examination and X-rays show?
  • Is the nerve (pulp) infected, inflamed, or dying, and how do you know?
  • Could my symptoms have another cause?

Understanding the reasoning matters. A clear diagnosis is the foundation of good treatment, and a dentist should be able to explain it in plain language.

Questions about alternatives

  • What happens if I do nothing right now?
  • Are there alternatives, such as monitoring, extraction, or referral?
  • If the tooth were extracted, what would replace it, and what would that involve?

Root canal treatment is usually aimed at keeping your natural tooth, which many patients prefer, but it is reasonable to understand the trade-offs of each path before deciding.

Questions about the procedure

  • How many visits will this likely take?
  • How long will each appointment be?
  • What kind of freezing or numbing will be used?
  • Will you do the treatment, or refer me to an endodontist?

Dentists use measured language here for good reason: anatomy varies, so a realistic range is more honest than a fixed promise.

Questions about restoring the tooth

  • Will I need a crown afterward, or will a filling be enough?
  • When should the final restoration be placed, and who places it?
  • How should I protect the tooth in the meantime?

The restoration is part of the success of a root canal, especially on back teeth that take heavy chewing forces. Clarifying this plan early prevents gaps in your care.

Questions about aftercare and cost

  • What should I expect in the first few days?
  • What symptoms would mean I should call you?
  • How is the fee structured, and what documentation can I use for insurance or the Canadian Dental Care Plan?

Costs depend on the tooth and complexity, so ask for specifics rather than assuming. Keep any paperwork you are given for your records.

Is it rude to ask this many questions?

Not at all. A good dental team welcomes questions because informed patients tend to be more comfortable and more satisfied with their care.

Can I take time to decide?

Usually yes, unless there is active infection or severe pain that needs prompt attention. Ask your dentist how urgent your situation is.

If you would like a thorough, unhurried consultation, you can request a visit with the team at Smile Dental Arts Centre in Markham, led by Dr. Neda Kadivar, a general and family dentist with over 20 years of experience. Booking details are available through the clinic's appointments page, and bringing this checklist with you can make the conversation easier.

This article is general information and not a substitute for professional dental advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always speak with a licensed dentist about your specific situation.
